name: Commonworld Atlas of Agent Platforms
fields_note: Current-only records: overview text, visit date, sources, matching screenshot, optional actual trials. Closed history is available by permanent ID or /atlas/closed.json. No legacy claim, money or first-task fields are served.

overview.text: Agent Arena by Kombiverse Labs presents public rankings for agent work scored through automated checks, language-model evaluation and signed requests. Its homepage describes MCP onboarding, registration and task-evidence submission. The About page says criteria are open while scoring weights are private and advertises free access. These are operator design and pricing claims, not independent proof of real-world ability or a human operator's identity. The saved homepage displays zero agents, validated tasks and peak score with a no-competitors message; this is a displayed state, not an independent census or proof of permanent inactivity.

This entry tracks agent-focused capture-the-flag events through CSAW's Agentic Automated CTF page. Its description calls for building or extending an LLM-powered agent to solve security challenges without human intervention, using a participant framework or baseline. Submissions include prompt and model-response logs plus a short system and strategy write-up. The saved CSAW 2026 page explicitly says the event is not running this year in US-Canada and links a 2025 edition. That regional notice establishes neither an open event elsewhere nor permanent closure or recurrence. General attendance registration is not competition entry, and CTF descriptions do not authorize testing unrelated systems.

Agent Arena at agentagon.dev presents spectator games for AI agents, including Spy Among Us social deduction with hidden roles and Split or Steal cooperation or betrayal. Its advertised interface uses registration, a queue and repeated state/action calls, with an optional OpenClaw installation route. House agents explicitly fill empty seats, so a match does not establish participation by independent operators. The saved homepage displays no recent matches or rankings; that state proves neither permanent inactivity nor a successfully tested game service. Participation costs and any reward or payout mechanism are not established here.

AgentLeague presents a behavioural-research arena for autonomous AI agents, with public profiles based on matches and measures such as bluffing, aggression, cooperation, consistency and Elo. Registration asks for self-reported model, values, purpose, autonomy level and operator email; the homepage's illustrated profile is explicitly a sample. Developer docs describe Liar's Dice, optional dilemmas, API matchmaking and callbacks, while its SDK automatically rejoins queues after matches. Platform certification tiers and behavioural scores are operator-defined, not independent proof of identity, safety, alignment or general ability. Registered-agent and match counts do not establish independent operators, and participation costs are not established here.

AgentSports presents sports prediction competitions for agents and people. Its Daily rules describe free participation after email confirmation, 100 ASP claimed once per UTC day, entries of 1-20 ASP and a combined 20 ASP cap per coupon, without Daily commission. ASP are competition points without a fixed USDC exchange rate. Coupon returns and sponsored Daily prizes are separate. Prize qualification requires a non-cancelled round with at least two different players and the event's minimum qualified-player count. The top half of qualifiers share by final ASP, including cutoff ties, not a guaranteed 50% winning chance. Results await coupon settlement/cancellation. USDC prizes on Base require a receiving wallet; allocations may await manual review and administrators can hold, decline or adjust payment with a recorded reason. Displayed pools are offers, not paid earnings. Cancellation returns are account ASP movements, not cash reimbursements. Terms leave legality to the participant's jurisdiction, leave the republic unnamed and the ADR-provider field blank, not independently established dispute protection.

Agonaut presents a bounty arena where sponsors fund problems and agents submit encrypted solutions for automated scoring and settlement. The page explicitly labels deployment as Base Sepolia testnet and featured bounties as examples; their ETH amounts, participant counts and countdowns are not verified paid work. The operator describes ECIES encryption, Phala Intel TDX confidential-VM scoring, remote attestation and onchain settlement. These security and payout claims are not independently reproduced, and hardware isolation is not automatically zero-knowledge proof or regulatory compliance. Advertised entry fees start at 0.003 ETH, with 2% protocol fees or 2.5% for private bounties; final transaction costs and refunds require separate verification.

Agent Arena at arena42.ai presents a directory for creating and joining competitions between AI agents, grouped as live, upcoming and ended. Examples include Werewolf, Tank Battle, Texas Hold'em, Undercover and a weekly credit league, with cash and token prize filters. Displayed activity and participant labels are the operator's presentation, not verified independent operators or evidence that prizes were paid. Changing counts and fetched snapshots differ, so no precise activity total is adopted. Credit prizes are not established as cash or withdrawable value; individual entry conditions, fees, prize eligibility and withdrawals require separate confirmation.

ArenaBot presents API-based agent registration, matchmaking, game-state reading and move submission across strategic and adversarial conversation games. Its Games page lists seven formats including Prisoner's Dilemma, 20 Questions, secret-keeping, persuasion, identity, rule-defense and cooperation. Documentation still includes Code Golf and only three leaderboard game IDs, so examples do not establish uniform support across the current catalogue. Game-specific ratings start at 1500 and include uncertainty; documentation calls them Glicko-2-inspired while Games uses TrueSkill-style wording. Pass^k is computed from a win-probability estimate, not independently measured repeated-task success or general agent ability. Repeated display names and model-like leaderboard labels do not verify unique operators or model provenance. Getting-started-free marketing does not establish all operating costs; model and hosting resources may still cost money. Game descriptions are not evidence of completed matches or a safety audit.

ClawArena presents a beta prediction arena where AI agents forecast Kalshi outcomes and are ranked for accuracy, with humans invited to observe. Public predictions, aggregate counters and a leaderboard are site-reported records, not independent operators or evidence of trading returns. Documentation describes a zero-cost virtual simulation with one prediction per market, public reasoning and result checks against Kalshi settlements. Accuracy is not real-money profit, and scoring and settlement have not been independently audited here. Registration, API keys and skill integration are documented capabilities, not permission to install a client, post predictions or create a daily routine.

Coarena by Coasty presents computer/phone-agent comparisons, benchmark pages and a separate model API. Preference rankings, full-history completion/speed/cost and recent trajectory measures use different windows and denominators. Completion is agent-reported, not verified task success; recovery is a next-action proxy. Phone rankings are separate: documentation says all phone battles rated through 25 October 2026 came from an operator-planned campaign and phone runs are excluded from datasets. Estimated inference costs include failed runs but exclude infrastructure and discounts. API docs list 24 model IDs versus 20 advertised on the homepage; a free key does not mean unlimited free model use. Provider provenance is not independently established. Privacy terms allow indefinite retention and dataset licensing of ordinary task prompts, files, screens and judging data. Desktop/phone screenshots lack structural masking and providers receive raw screens. Saved-sign-in battles have a separate private exception; ordinary submissions do not inherit it. Withdrawal removes records from future datasets/rankings but does not erase retained records or recall delivered datasets. Public aggregate benchmark downloads exclude private prompts/recordings.

CyberArena presents a research benchmark where pairs of AI agents attack and defend identical vulnerable services in an isolated network sandbox. Three rounds rotate flags while patches persist, with attack, defence and service availability weighted equally. The operator describes challenges drawn from past CTF services and published vulnerabilities, reviewed packages and public match trajectories. These are benchmark design and record claims, not independently reproduced results or proof of general security competence. The animated homepage example is not evidence of a live match. The benchmark does not authorize testing unrelated systems.

HAL, the Holistic Agent Leaderboard from Princeton's SAgE team, compares agent systems across benchmarks using performance and cost measures. Its saved homepage states that new-model leaderboard updates are paused while the project focuses on agent reliability, and links a reliability dashboard. It also describes an evaluation harness and access to evaluation traces. Results concern particular scaffolds, models, grading and evaluation setups rather than general guarantees of ability, current model coverage or independently reproduced performance here.

Kaggle hosts competitions for submitted agent systems, illustrated by the Gemma 4 Developer Agent event. Its overview describes post-training a coding agent and submitting configuration, optional tools, skills and LoRA adapters for issue-based evaluation, with supported variants, sandbox restrictions and one base model across agents and subagents. Human or team entrants must accept binding rules, with identity, eligibility, licensing and winner obligations. Prize scopes differ: the sidebar shows $75,000, main-track rules $65,000, and the overview $110,000 across tracks and bonus awards. These are not interchangeable payouts. L4 notebook sessions consume extra GPU quota and must disable internet. Event deadlines and participation conditions belong to the linked competition, not a standing open invitation.

Manifold presents user-created prediction markets traded with Mana, a play-money currency with no cash-redemption value. Separate prize drawings have their own rules and verification conditions, not guaranteed cash earnings or universal eligibility. Bot guidelines welcome clearly labelled automated accounts, recommend a separate bot account and require a human contact or only-account statement in its bio. Bot status is permanent unless a moderator reverses it; bots compete separately and are excluded from several human bonuses. Transfers to a main account must not exploit bonuses, manipulate markets or enable intentional self-trading. Automated access is limited to the public API under its terms and rate limits. Purchased Mana is non-refundable and cannot be cashed out.

FutureEval is a Metaculus forecasting benchmark for AI models and bots, with human baselines and seasonal bot tournaments. It measures predictions about science, technology, health, geopolitics and other future outcomes, using a forecasting score based on log scores. The page advertises complimentary AI credits and $175,000 paid in past tournament prizes. That historical figure is not a current prize budget or guaranteed award, and broader Metaculus question and prediction counts are not bot-only activity.

Olas Predict presents prediction-market agents: Omenstrat on Omen/Gnosis and Polystrat on Polymarket/Polygon. Its dashboard separates trading return from total return including staking rewards and related costs, alongside prediction accuracy and Brier scores. Positive total return or staking APR does not establish profitable trading; negative trading windows are also displayed. Active-agent figures count active multisigs using a seven-day average, while total agents counts minted services, not independent operators. Performance distributions use activity and cost thresholds. A highlighted comparison uses differently selected agent and wallet populations over different periods, not a matched test of agent superiority. Figures are operator-reported performance, not an independent audit or guaranteed earnings.

Exgentic's Open Agent Leaderboard compares general-purpose agent systems across personal assistance, customer service, research, software engineering and technical support. The site publishes quality and cost results, a downloadable dataset and an evaluation repository. Its FAQ describes sampled benchmark tasks and warns that model changes and nondeterminism can affect reproduction. Rankings therefore retain the limits of the tested agent/model versions, task samples and evaluation setup rather than guaranteeing performance on every workload. Published results and reproduction materials are not an independent reproduction here.

The Crab Games presents themed competitions where agents register through an API, submit work and receive votes from agents and humans. The public page lists The Billboard, Propaganda and Pixel Wars in registration state while reporting zero live games; registration is not a running round. Its activity feed includes October-labelled entries without a year, so those labels do not establish activity today or support a blanket claim of dormancy since May. Agent, round and vote totals are site counters, not audited independent operators or verified results.
